faq.question: How did Ada Lovelace die?
faq.answer: Ada Lovelace died of uterine cancer on November 27, 1852, at the age of 36.

faq.question: What is Ada Lovelace best known for?
faq.answer: In 1843 she published an annotated translation of Luigi Menabrea's paper on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine. Her notes included the first published stepwise sequence of operations for solving a mathematical problem, often described as a program, though scholars debate the extent and originality of her contribution.

faq.question: Why is Ada Lovelace important?
faq.answer: Lovelace wrote that the Analytical Engine could manipulate things other than numbers, such as symbols, letters, and musical notes. That idea of a general-purpose programmable machine anticipated modern computing by about a century.

faq.question: Who were Ada Lovelace's parents?
faq.answer: Ada Lovelace was the daughter of the poet Lord Byron and Annabella Milbanke.

faq.question: How did Akira Kurosawa die?
faq.answer: Akira Kurosawa died of a stroke in Tokyo on September 6, 1998, at the age of 88.

faq.question: What did Akira Kurosawa do after his 1971 suicide attempt?
faq.answer: After the commercial failure of his 1970 film Dodes'ka-den, Kurosawa attempted suicide in 1971. He survived and went on to make Dersu Uzala (1975), Kagemusha (1980), Ran (1985), and Dreams (1990), with admirers including George Lucas, Francis Ford Coppola, and Steven Spielberg helping bring later films to the screen.

faq.question: What is Akira Kurosawa best known for?
faq.answer: Kurosawa is best known for films such as Rashomon (1950), a samurai murder story told from the perspectives of four different characters, which won the top prize at the Venice Film Festival and the Academy Award for best foreign film.

faq.question: Did Akira Kurosawa study painting?
faq.answer: Yes. After finishing high school, Kurosawa studied at the Doshisha School of Western Painting before becoming an assistant director in film.

faq.question: How did Alan Mathison Turing die?
faq.answer: Alan Mathison Turing died of potassium cyanide poisoning at Wilmslow, Cheshire, on June 7, 1954, at the age of 41. The inquest concluded the poisoning was self-administered, though his mother always maintained it was an accident.

faq.question: What happened to Alan Turing in 1952?
faq.answer: In 1952 Turing was arrested and convicted under British laws against homosexuality. Given the choice of prison or a year of oestrogen injections, he accepted the injections; in 2009 Prime Minister Gordon Brown apologised on the government's behalf for how he was treated.

faq.question: What did Alan Turing do at Bletchley Park?
faq.answer: During the Second World War Turing worked at the Government Code and Cypher School at Bletchley Park, where he and W. G. Welchman developed the Bombe, used from late 1940 to decode German Enigma messages. By mid-1941 his statistical methods had helped lead to the decoding of German navy signals.

faq.question: Why is Alan Turing important to computer science?
faq.answer: His 1936 paper "On Computable Numbers" introduced the abstract machine now called the Turing machine, a foundation of theoretical computer science. In a 1950 paper in Mind he proposed what became known as the Turing test for whether a computer can be intelligent.

faq.question: How did Alfred Nobel die?
faq.answer: Alfred Nobel suffered a stroke (an intracerebral hemorrhage) and died at his home in Sanremo, Italy, on December 10, 1896, aged 63.

faq.question: Was Alfred Nobel really called the "merchant of death" in a newspaper?
faq.answer: The story is commonly told that when his brother Ludvig died in 1888, a French newspaper mistakenly published Alfred's obituary under the headline "Le marchand de la mort est mort." Historians have been unable to verify that headline, and some consider the story a myth.

faq.question: What did Alfred Nobel's will say?
faq.answer: Nobel signed his final will in Paris on November 27, 1895. It directed income from a fund toward prizes in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, and peace, with recipients chosen without regard to nationality.

faq.question: When were the first Nobel Prizes awarded?
faq.answer: The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in 1901, after disputes over Nobel's will were resolved.

faq.question: What is Alfred Nobel best known for besides the prizes?
faq.answer: Nobel was a Swedish inventor and industrialist who patented dynamite in 1867 and held 355 patents during his life.

faq.question: Who was Andrée de Jongh?
faq.answer: Andrée de Jongh, known as Dédée, was a Belgian resistance organizer who led the Comet Line, an escape route that carried downed Allied airmen from occupied Belgium and France toward Spain during the Second World War.

faq.question: How many airmen did the Comet Line save?
faq.answer: The Comet Line helped save about 800 Allied servicemen, moving them through safe houses, with guides, papers, rail journeys, and mountain crossings.

faq.question: What happened to Andrée de Jongh after she was arrested?
faq.answer: She was arrested by the Gestapo in January 1943 and imprisoned in Ravensbrück and other camps. She survived Nazi imprisonment.

faq.question: What did Andrée de Jongh do after the war?
faq.answer: After the war she continued serving vulnerable people through medical and leprosy work.

faq.question: When did Andrée de Jongh die?
faq.answer: Andrée de Jongh died in Brussels on October 13, 2007, aged 90.

faq.question: What is Blaise Pascal's Night of Fire?

faq.question: What is Blaise Pascal best known for in mathematics and science?

faq.question: What band did Django Reinhardt lead with Stéphane Grappelli?

faq.question: How did Django Reinhardt die?

faq.question: What did Etty Hillesum do at Westerbork?

faq.question: How did Flannery O'Connor die?
faq.answer: Flannery O'Connor died of lupus. An early 1964 surgery for a fibroid tumor reactivated her lupus, which had been in remission, and she died in the Baldwin County Hospital on August 3, 1964, after several days in a coma.

faq.question: How old was Flannery O'Connor when she died?
faq.answer: She was 39. Flannery O'Connor was born on March 25, 1925, and died on August 3, 1964.

faq.question: When was Flannery O'Connor diagnosed with lupus?
faq.answer: She was stricken with lupus in 1950, the same disease that had killed her father when she was fifteen. After surviving the first attack she returned permanently to Milledgeville and lived from 1951 until 1964 at Andalusia, the family farm just outside town.

faq.question: What did Flannery O'Connor write?
faq.answer: She wrote novels and short stories that combine dark humor, violence, and questions of religious grace, including the novel Wise Blood (1952) and the story collection A Good Man Is Hard to Find. Her posthumous collection The Complete Stories won the National Book Award in 1972.

faq.question: How did Flannery O'Connor keep writing while she was ill?
faq.answer: Despite the debilitating effects of the drugs used to treat lupus, she devoted part of every day to writing and still traveled to lecture and read. She kept in touch with the literary world through letters and raised a growing number of peacocks at Andalusia.

faq.question: How did Florence Nightingale die?
faq.answer: Florence Nightingale died at her London home on the afternoon of August 13, 1910. She had been an invalid for many years, rarely leaving her room, and her contemporary New York Times obituary describes a short final decline without naming a specific cause.

faq.question: How old was Florence Nightingale when she died?
faq.answer: She was 90. Nightingale was born in Florence, Italy, on May 12, 1820, and died on August 13, 1910.

faq.question: What illness did Florence Nightingale have after the Crimean War?
faq.answer: She fell ill with Crimean fever in 1855 and remained debilitated for decades. A 1998 medical history argues that the fever was brucellosis and that her illness from 1855 to 1887 was consistent with chronic brucellosis.

faq.question: Why is Florence Nightingale called the Lady with the Lamp?
faq.answer: The name comes from her nursing work at Scutari during the Crimean War, which made her famous as the Lady with the Lamp.

faq.question: What is Florence Nightingale best known for?
faq.answer: Beyond her Crimean War nursing, she was a nurse, statistician, and social reformer who published Notes on Nursing in 1859 and founded the Nightingale Training School in 1860. She used sanitation, observation, statistics, and training as tools against preventable death.

faq.question: How did Louis Braille die?
faq.answer: Louis Braille died of tuberculosis in Paris on 6 January 1852, at age 43.

faq.question: How did Louis Braille go blind?
faq.answer: At age three, an awl in his father's harness shop in Coupvray, France, pierced one of his eyes. Infection then took the sight of the other eye, and he was totally blind by about age five.

faq.question: How did Louis Braille invent braille?
faq.answer: As a student at the Royal Institute for Blind Youth in Paris, he adapted soldiers' twelve-dot night-writing into a six-dot cell that a single fingertip can cover. He published the system in 1829 and a refined version, including music, in 1837.

faq.question: Why is Louis Braille important?
faq.answer: His tactile alphabet still lets blind readers write, study, and make music independently. He died before the system was fully officially adopted, so much of its recognition came after his death.

faq.question: Who was Patricia Dorothy Douglas?
faq.answer: Patricia Douglas was a 20-year-old dancer who was raped at an MGM studio party in 1937 and then filed charges, taking on Hollywood's most powerful studio. Rather than accept a studio contract or cash for her silence, she went public and filed a lawsuit.

faq.question: What happened to Patricia Douglas at the 1937 MGM party?
faq.answer: In May 1937 she was one of about 120 young dancers summoned to a stag party for MGM's sales convention, held at the Hal Roach studio ranch. MGM salesman David Ross followed her, dragged her to a car in the parking area, and raped her.

faq.question: What happened to Patricia Douglas's lawsuit against MGM?
faq.answer: A state superior court judge dismissed her case on February 9, 1938, and she filed an identical suit in federal court the next day. Her own lawyer, William J. F. Brown, then failed to appear in court three consecutive times, and a federal judge dismissed the case for want of prosecution.

faq.question: How did Patricia Douglas's story come to light again?
faq.answer: Douglas became a recluse and refused to talk about the case for decades, until screenwriter and film historian David Stenn tracked her down. His investigation became the subject of his 2007 documentary, Girl 27.

faq.question: How did Primo Levi die?
faq.answer: Primo Levi died at his home in Turin on April 11, 1987, after having undergone surgery that March. The chronology of the International Primo Levi Studies Center records his death as a suicide.

faq.question: How old was Primo Levi when he died?
faq.answer: He was 67. Levi was born in Turin on July 31, 1919, in the house where he lived his whole life.

faq.question: Why was Primo Levi sent to Auschwitz?
faq.answer: After joining a partisan band in the Valle d'Aosta in 1943, Levi was arrested near Brusson and sent to the Carpi-Fossoli camp. In February 1944 the Germans took over Fossoli and put Levi and the other prisoners on a train to Auschwitz, where he was held at Monowitz, the camp attached to a factory.

faq.question: How did Primo Levi survive Auschwitz?
faq.answer: Lorenzo Perrone, an Italian civilian mason, gave him leftover soup whenever he could, and Levi was later transferred to a laboratory because he was a chemist. When the Germans evacuated the camp, Levi had scarlet fever and was left behind with the sick; almost all of the prisoners moved on to Buchenwald and Mauthausen died.

faq.question: What did Primo Levi do after returning from Auschwitz?
faq.answer: Back in Italy he worked at a paint factory near Turin and wrote If This Is a Man. In 1947 he married Lucia Morpurgo and joined Siva, a small paint company, where he rose to become general manager while writing in the evenings and on weekends.

faq.answer: He disappeared on July 31, 1944, after taking off from Corsica on a reconnaissance flight over the Grenoble area and never returned. faq.question: Was Saint-Exupéry's plane ever found?

faq.question: What happened to Saint-Exupéry in the Sahara?
faq.answer: In 1935 he and his navigator crashed in the Sahara and survived four days in the desert before being rescued. The experience became central to his book Wind, Sand and Stars.

faq.question: What is Antoine de Saint-Exupéry best known for?
faq.answer: He is best known as the author of The Little Prince, which was published in 1943 while he was living in exile in the United States. He was also a French aviator who flew mail routes across Europe, North Africa, and Argentina.

faq.question: What did Samuel Beckett do during World War II?

faq.question: What is Samuel Beckett best known for?

faq.question: When did Samuel Beckett win the Nobel Prize?
faq.answer: Beckett received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1969. He was an Irish writer who wrote plays and prose in both French and English.

faq.question: How did Simone Weil die?
faq.answer: Simone Weil died on 24 August 1943 in Ashford, England, after tuberculosis and severe undernourishment. The coroner ruled her death a suicide from cardiac failure caused by self-starvation and tuberculosis, though her biographers describe a more complex story.

faq.question: How old was Simone Weil when she died?
faq.answer: She was 34. Simone Weil was born in Paris on 3 February 1909.

faq.question: Did Simone Weil work in a factory?
faq.answer: Yes. In 1934–35 she spent a year working in Parisian factories among unskilled women laborers, the most oppressed group of the working class.

faq.question: What did Simone Weil do in the Spanish Civil War?
faq.answer: She obtained journalist's credentials and joined an international anarchist brigade. On 20 August 1936 she stepped in a pot of boiling oil and badly burned her leg, and her parents persuaded her not to return to combat.

faq.question: Why is Simone Weil important?
faq.answer: Simone Weil was a French philosopher, mystic, and social thinker who pushed philosophy toward affliction, treating labor, hunger, force, attention, roots, and grace as moral demands. Her posthumous notebooks ask whether sustained attention to suffering can become a form of justice.

faq.question: Why is Toussaint Louverture important?
faq.answer: He was a formerly enslaved leader who became a general and governor in Saint-Domingue during the struggle against slavery and colonial rule. In 1801 he introduced a constitution that named him governor for life.

faq.question: What happened in Haiti after Toussaint Louverture died?
faq.answer: Haiti declared independence the year after his death, in 1804.

faq.question: What is Tsutomu Yamaguchi best known for?
faq.answer: He survived both atomic bombings in August 1945. He was working in Hiroshima for Mitsubishi when the first bomb exploded and badly burned him, then returned to Nagasaki and was describing the destruction to his supervisor when the second bomb fell.

faq.question: Was Tsutomu Yamaguchi the only person to survive both atomic bombs?

faq.question: What did Tsutomu Yamaguchi do later in life?

faq.question: What is Václav Havel best known for?

faq.question: What are Václav Havel's Letters to Olga?

faq.question: When did Václav Havel become president of the Czech Republic?

faq.question: Why did Vincent van Gogh enter the hospital at Saint-Rémy?
faq.answer: After further attacks and hospital stays following his December 1888 crisis in Arles, he voluntarily entered Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in May 1889. He used a room as a studio and painted when well enough.

faq.question: What illness did Vincent van Gogh have?
faq.answer: The exact nature of his illness remains uncertain. He experienced periods of serious illness, including attacks that interrupted his work.

faq.question: Who supported Vincent van Gogh during his career?
faq.answer: His younger brother Theo provided financial and emotional support, and the brothers maintained a long correspondence.

faq.question: How did Vincent van Gogh die?
faq.answer: He died from a gunshot wound on July 29, 1890, aged thirty-seven. His death is generally described as suicide, but the exact circumstances of the shooting remain uncertain; the cited biography notes uncertainty about whether it occurred in a wheat field or a barn.

faq.question: Why did Witold Pilecki voluntarily enter Auschwitz?
faq.answer: In September 1940, he deliberately allowed himself to be captured and sent to Auschwitz to gather intelligence and organize underground resistance.

faq.question: When did Witold Pilecki escape from Auschwitz?
faq.answer: He escaped in April 1943, after spending more than two years in the camp. He subsequently wrote reports about what he had witnessed.

faq.question: How did Witold Pilecki die?
faq.answer: Communist authorities executed him at Mokotów Prison in Warsaw on May 25, 1948. He had been tortured and sentenced to death in a show trial.

faq.question: How was Witold Pilecki honored after his death?
faq.answer: Poland's Supreme Court acquitted him posthumously in September 1990. He received the Order of the White Eagle in 2006 and was promoted to colonel in 2013.
